name: Fatima Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ines and I own Brook End, ninety hectares of sheep, wheat and vegetables. In lambing I'm out every three hours through the night, but on a normal day I check the 300 ewes at seven, then it's the veg beds, carrots and leeks mostly, which we sell through the Green Vale co-op. Our son Tomás works with us three days a week. Afternoons I'm often at the kitchen table with the co-op paperwork.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the mornings with the flock, when the mist is still down by the brook. What wears me out is the price squeeze. The supermarket that buys from the co-op knocks a few pence off every year, and fertiliser and diesel go the other way. I've started using one of those AI chat tools now and then to tidy up grant forms, which saves me an evening, but that's as far as I've gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at co-op meetings: the problem was never the technology, it's who holds the buying power. If AI changes nothing, the supermarket still sets our price. I might post that in the co-op's group chat, with a few too many exclamation marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means the same pressures we already have. The farm makes decent money, and we've got savings and the land, so we're not in trouble. But every year the margin on lamb gets thinner, and that's on my mind whether AI is a flop or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what we're doing and keep pushing the co-op to negotiate as a block. I'd carry on using the chat tool for grant forms, nothing more. And I'd keep going with the plan to hand Brook End to Tomás by about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. I'd half hoped it might at least take the paperwork off me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the pressure you'd still be carrying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarket letter comes every spring, and my wife Ines reads it first so I don't throw it in the fire. That letter would still come in AI Plateau, and it would still say less money for the same carrots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomás and your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter Clara teaches at the primary school, and in AI Plateau her job stays the same, so that's fine. Tomás is the one I think about, because the farm has to support him and his partner when we step back. I'd tell Tomás the farm is his if he wants it, but the co-op is what keeps it alive.

say: The problem was never technology, it's who holds the **buying power**.
Even if AI changes nothing, the **supermarket** still sets our price.
think: We're not in trouble, with **savings and the land** behind us.
The **lamb margin** gets thinner every year, AI or no AI.
do: Push the co-op to **negotiate as a block** with the supermarket.
Keep using the chat tool for **grant forms**, and nothing more.
Stick with the plan to **hand over** Brook End to Tomás around 2031.
feel: A bit **flat**, since she'd hoped AI might lift the paperwork.
S0.quote: The supermarket letter comes every spring, and my wife Ines reads it first so I don't throw it in the fire.
fieldNote: Her worry predates AI: the **supermarket squeeze** on lamb and veg prices.
Sees the **co-op** as the answer to most problems.
The **handover to Tomás** frames every choice she describes.

steps.text: Push the Green Vale co-op to negotiate lamb prices as one block
Keep lambing, veg beds and the handover plan to Tomás

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when farmers need to stick together. If AI is doing the buying and the planning for the supermarkets, then the co-op needs it too, or we get eaten. I'd say that at the co-op meeting and probably write it up for the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For Brook End, the thinking jobs are mine: the orders, the grant forms, the planting plan, the lamb sales. If AI can do those well, that's my kitchen-table afternoons back. The hands-on work, the lambing and the leeks, stays ours for a good while, so I'm not losing my living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever course the co-op runs on AI farm records, once a few others had tried it. Within the year I'd want the planting plan and the sheep records on one system. And I'd push the co-op to buy one shared AI service for price data, so we're not each paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's a hopeful bit in it too. It could take the drudgery, if we're not the ones being squeezed by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's sitting on the other side of the table in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big chains will have AI first, and better. The supermarket buyers will know our costs before we do. That's what I'd worry about: not the tool, but the other side of the table using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gemma at the co-op office, she does our grading sheets and sales invoices. If software does that, the co-op saves money but Gemma's hours get cut. I'd argue for keeping her on, doing something else, like visiting farms to help us set the systems up.

say: Farmers need to **stick together** now more than ever.
If supermarkets use AI to buy, the **co-op needs it too**, or we get eaten.
think: AI could take my **kitchen-table afternoons** of forms and orders.
The **lambing and the leeks** stay ours, so our living is safe for now.
do: Join the co-op's **AI records course** once others have tried it.
Get the **planting plan** and sheep records onto one system within a year.
Push the co-op to share **one AI service** for price data.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a hopeful streak about losing the **drudgery**.
S1.quote: The supermarket buyers will know our costs before we do.
fieldNote: Separates the **thinking parts** of her job, which she'd gladly hand over, from the hands-on parts.
Her real fear is the **buyer's advantage**, not losing her own work.
Speaks up for **Gemma** in the co-op office before anyone asks.

steps.text: Take the co-op's course on AI farm records next winter
Ask the co-op to buy one shared AI price service
Keep lambing and growing leeks and carrots as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public rules, fast, and public money to help small farms share the new machines. Otherwise the big agribusinesses buy the robots in 2031 and the rest of us are finished on price. I'd be at the co-op, at the farmers' union, and yes, I'd finally go on social media about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it squeezes us from both ends. From 2028, the supermarkets and big farms plan and buy with AI that's sharper than any of us. Then around 2031, their robots do the field work for less than we pay Tomás, and our lamb and veg are worth even less. We wouldn't go hungry, but Brook End might stop paying its way just as Tomás takes over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd get the co-op to start a fund to buy shared robots, so we have them in 2031 and not only the big boys. I'd use the AI myself from 2028 for all the paperwork and the selling, no point being proud. And I'd sit down with Tomás and Ines and decide whether we still hand over in 2031, or hold off and keep savings back in case he needs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not my own wage, it's whether the farm I've built is worth anything to my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ines say to each other that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would say, let's sell the top forty hectares while land's still worth something. I'd say no, the land's the one thing they can't make more of. We'd probably argue about it until two in the morning and then go and check the ewes together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the new tractor. We were going to replace the old Massey next year for about 60,000, and I'd stop that dead and keep the money for whatever the co-op robot scheme costs. No point buying a machine that drives itself worse than the one coming in three years.

say: We need **public rules**, fast, and money to help small farms **share machines**.
Otherwise **big agribusiness** buys the robots and the rest of us are finished on price.
think: From **2028** the big buyers plan and price with sharper AI than ours.
From **2031** their robots undercut our lamb and veg, just as Tomás takes over.
do: Start a **co-op fund** to buy shared robots before 2031.
Use AI for **all the paperwork** and selling from 2028.
Drop the **60,000** Massey replacement and rethink the handover with Tomás.
feel: **Anxious** about whether the farm she built is worth anything to her son.
S2.quote: We were going to replace the old Massey next year for about 60,000, and I'd stop that dead and keep the money for whatever the co-op robot scheme costs.
fieldNote: Sees the **gap years** as a squeeze: AI-powered buyers first, robot farms after.
Her answer is **shared ownership** of machines through the co-op.
A real **disagreement** with Ines about selling land surfaced on its own.

steps.text: Set up a Green Vale co-op fund for shared farm robots
Ask the farmers' union to lobby for small-farm machine grants
Rethink the 2031 handover of Brook End with Tomás

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if farmers organise now. I'd tell the co-op: we have until 2031 for the thinking side and 2034 for the robots, so let's use it. It's the same message as the fast one, just less shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the handover to Tomás would land right in the middle of it. He'd take over Brook End around 2031, just as the AI changes buying and planning, and then the robots come in 2034. I'd be 66 and stepping back, but I'd still be living on the farm and drawing from it, so its income is my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years I'd put about 20,000 into the co-op's shared machine fund and get Tomás onto its board. I'd learn the AI planning tools properly with him, so he isn't doing it alone. And we'd agree that Ines and I keep a bigger cash cushion until 2034 instead of putting it all into the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but steadier. There's time to make a plan, and I'm the kind who likes to see a thing working on someone else's farm first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomás want to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás would say, Mum, let's just buy our own robot. I'd tell him to wait and see what the co-op does. I'd tell my son Tomás to look at the Hendersons' farm first, because the Hendersons always buy everything first. If it works for them, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said your income is the farm's income. What happens to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our income would probably drop by a third once the robot farms set the price, that's my guess, though I honestly don't know. We'd manage on savings and my pension. What I don't know is whether Tomás would want to stay if the farm earns less than a teaching wage like his sister's.

say: Five years is **enough time** if farmers organise now.
We have until **2031** for the thinking side and **2034** for robots.
think: The **handover to Tomás** lands right in the middle of the change.
Brook End's **income is my income**, even after I step back.
do: Put about **20,000** into the co-op's shared machine fund.
Learn the **AI planning tools** alongside Tomás.
Keep a **bigger cash cushion** until 2034 rather than reinvesting it all.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, because there's time to see things work first.
S3.quote: I'd tell my son Tomás to look at the Hendersons' farm first, because the Hendersons always buy everything first.
fieldNote: Her **steady** streak shows: she wants to see robots work on a **neighbour's farm** first.
Guesses farm income could **drop by a third**, and admits she doesn't really know.
Worries whether her son would **stay** if farming pays less than teaching.

steps.text: Put about 20,000 into the co-op's shared machine fund
Learn the AI planning tools side by side with Tomás
Keep a larger cash cushion until the robots arrive in 2034
Get Tomás a seat on the co-op board before the handover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to build it right: co-op-owned machines, training for farm workers, and land kept in family hands. I'd keep saying it at every meeting until people were sick of me. I'd also say we should be grateful, because ten years is more than most changes give you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it's mostly after my time. I hand over in 2031, the thinking AI comes in 2036 and robots about 2039. It's Tomás who has to live through it, and he'd be in his forties with a farm that's his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand over to Tomás on schedule and help him write a ten-year plan for Brook End. I'd learn enough of the AI tools by then to help him with the planning side while I'm still around. And I'd put some of our savings into the co-op machine fund, slowly, as the robots get proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Tomás, calm for me. It's a strange mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás when you hand him the keys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomás the farm isn't a museum, he should change it however he needs to. I'd also tell him not to sell the brook meadow, because my mother is buried in the churchyard right above it. That's the one thing I'd ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the co-op to do with the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the co-op to spend the first five years on training, not on machines. The machines will be cheaper by 2039 anyway. People take longer to change than tractors do.

say: A decade is time to **build it right**, with co-op machines and training.
Ten years is **more warning** than most changes give you.
think: Most of this lands **after my time**, once I hand over in 2031.
**Tomás** lives through it, in his forties with a farm of his own.
do: Hand Brook End to Tomás **on schedule** in 2031.
Help write a **ten-year plan** and learn enough AI to help with planning.
Move savings into the **co-op machine fund** slowly as robots prove themselves.
feel: **Uneasy** for her son and **calm** for herself, an odd mix.
S4.quote: People take longer to change than tractors do.
fieldNote: The long warning shifts her worry almost entirely onto **Tomás**.
Her one fixed wish is to keep the **brook meadow**, tied to her mother's grave.
Would put **training before machines**, a clear progressive priority.

steps.text: Hand Brook End to Tomás in 2031 with a written ten-year plan
Move savings into the co-op machine fund as robots prove themselves

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because we'd starve, we wouldn't, but because it hits just as Tomás takes over and before the co-op has a plan. What would help is public money for co-ops to buy shared robots, and a rule that supermarkets can't use AI to push prices below what it costs us to grow the food.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land itself. When farms stop paying, they get sold to whoever has the most money, and that's never the family down the road. Farmland should go to people who farm it, robots or not.

headlineQuote: Farmland should go to people who farm it, robots or not.
portrait: A 58-year-old **sheep and veg** farmer who owns Brook End with her wife Ines.
Plans to **hand the farm** to her son Tomás around 2031, and frames every choice around that.
Puts her faith in the **Green Vale co-op**, shared machines and public rules on supermarkets.
Uses AI **now and then** for forms, and wants to see robots work on a neighbour's farm first.
Uneasy in mild pictures, **anxious** when AGI lands near the handover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits as Tomás takes over and before the co-op has a plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for co-ops to buy shared robots.
A rule stopping supermarkets using AI to push prices **below growing costs**.
